description.description: Framed as a stewardship log rather than a budgeting app: the question it answers is 'have I given first,' not 'how much did I spend.' Single user by design.
Throwaway prototype kept as the canonical reference for layout, copy and flow only — explicitly not architecture, so its code is never a model to copy.
No native app. Logging must work with no network, because a log that fails when offline is a log that never happens.
Acceptance criterion for v1: log a real expense in under 5 seconds, offline, and see it correctly in Month after a reload. Chosen as a single falsifiable bar rather than a list of features.
Currency is PHP only, 'no multi-currency, ever' — removes rate-at-time-of-transaction and cross-currency-total questions entirely.
All copy in formal English, no Tagalog: 'Motor upkeep' not 'motor gastos', 'Money borrowed and lent' not 'utang at pautang'.
Manna deploys separately from Tiswell but shares Tiswell's database, so one capture surface is not blocked on the other's release cycle.
Amount, category (parent + optional subcategory), wallet, date, optional note, kind. debt_id and a no-category flag are added in v1 so the v1.5 Owed screen needs no migration.
Transfers never appear in category totals. Moving money to savings and paying down a debt both drop cash without consuming anything, so counting them as spending would make the reports lie.
GCash, Cash, Maribank, GoTyme, Wise, Savings. Savings is a wallet and not a category; the Wallets grand total must answer 'what can I spend today', so anything not spendable stays out of it.

Expense parents: Food, Transportation, Housing & Utilities, Communication & Tech, Health, Personal, Giving, Learning, Leisure, Financial, Work. Income parents: Earned, Business, Passive, Other. Each parent owns a colour and an icon, both editable in Settings.

Person, direction (owe/owed), principal, opened date, optional due date, status. Payments are not new objects — they are transactions carrying a debt_id and no category — so balance is principal minus linked payments and partial payments need no extra code.
A template of category, amount, wallet and day of month that generates a monthly proposal; it does not create a transaction until approved.
A cap on a category — except Giving, which is a floor instead of a ceiling. That inversion is where the stewardship function lives.
If a sub-sub is wanted, it is a note or a tag. Icon resolution is what makes this cost nothing visually: two levels still give every row a distinct shape.
Parents must fit one screen with no scrolling because a parent is picked on every log; a 13th is refused.
Logging to a bare parent must be one tap — a hurried log that gets sorted later beats a log that never happened.

'Jollibee' goes in the note field; merchants as categories grow without limit and make reports meaningless. Currently unenforced — nothing counts three occurrences before allowing a new subcategory, and this is flagged as the rule most worth automating.

A subcategory has no colour or icon of its own; colour is inherited outright, while the icon resolves by the sub's own name first ('Dental' gets a tooth, not Health's heartbeat), then the parent's, then a fallback tag.

Icons live in one catalogue in src/icons.tsx keyed by stable strings ('utensils', not a component). The key is what is stored on the category, so the underlying icon library can be swapped by editing that one file.
Spendable total, reminders, month summary with pace against average, allotments running hot, today's transactions. Also carries the tithe strip.
Six-month in/out chart, then categories ranked by amount with their subcategory breakdown.

Full-screen sheet from the centre button with a built-in numpad rather than the system keyboard, because the system keyboard covers the categories and forces you to type blind. Amount, note, wallet and categories are all visible at once.
Three tabs — Expected (approve or skip), Allotments (progress), Considering. Plan shows status, Settings holds the rules; Plan is deliberately not editable.
Balances, spendable grand total, and a separate Owed panel kept out of that total.
Debts and loans in both directions with payment history. Scheduled for v1.5, but its schema hooks land in v1 to avoid a migration.
Categories, Recurring, Allotments, General. Settings holds the rules — it is the only place they can be edited.
Only a handful of PH banks are reachable by any aggregator, and those aggregators are B2B with contracts and compliance onboarding — not available to a solo developer.

If capture is ever automated it will be SMS or notification parsing on Android via MacroDroid or a small sideloaded listener posting to the API, which keeps Manna a pure PWA rather than forcing a native app.
Silent monthly deductions are exactly the passivity the app exists to work against. The amount stays editable at the moment of approval, because bills vary.
It existed, was then derived from the category, then removed entirely. Categories are the only classification and the split must not be reintroduced.

Giving gets no special data-model status. The stewardship function is carried by exactly two things: the tithe strip on Home, and the Giving allotment being a floor while every other allotment is a ceiling.
Manna owns money that moves; Tiswell owns things you have. A to-buy is money about to move, a to-sell is a possession — that is the boundary between the two apps.
Money lent out cannot be spent. Rolling it in would turn the grand total into net worth, which answers a different question than 'what can I spend today'.
No bank sync, no multi-currency, no receipt photos, no business ledger, no merchant-level categories, no third category level.

v1 core ledger and screens; v1.1 recurring with approval, allotments, search, CSV export; v1.5 Owed. debt_id (nullable) and the no-category flag go into the v1 transaction schema specifically so v1.5 needs no migration.
Undecided whether moving a category between parents rewrites history or applies going forward only. Flagged to be picked deliberately rather than falling out of an implementation.
Named for the daily bread provided in the wilderness — provision, one day at a time. Its own app on its own origin in the Tiswell family.
Type an amount and hit Add; category and wallet come from whatever you used last, so the common case is two taps. Any row can be tapped afterwards to correct it.
In / out / net, where the money went, and arrows back through past months.
A balance per wallet and a grand total.
Floats would drift a centavo at a time through the sums, and a ledger that doesn't add up is worse than none.
Shifts both wallet balances but is excluded from month totals and the category breakdown: PHP 2,000 moved from cash to GCash is not PHP 2,000 earned and PHP 2,000 spent.
The edit sheet is what makes amount-only logging safe rather than sloppy — speed on entry is only acceptable because correction afterwards is one tap.

Tiswell does not compile Manna in; it appears as an embedded tile pointed at an origin. Embedded, Manna adopts the host's session over postMessage (@data/handshake) so there is no second sign-in; opened standalone it shows its own sign-in and reaches the same data.

Storage is a shared InstantDB app rather than per-origin browser storage, so a transaction logged in Manna and a capture jotted in Tiswell live in the same place and both sync to every device. VITE_INSTANT_APP_ID being the identical string in both repos is literally what makes them one database; VITE_TISWELL_ORIGIN allowlists which origins a session is accepted from.

Borrows Tiswell's tokens, UI components and TiswellData layer as source via vite aliases pointing at ../TisWell/src, so the app always looks unmistakably Tiswell. Cost: both folders must sit side by side even to build. resolve.dedupe keeps react and @instantdb/react to a single copy each.
Default categories and a Cash wallet are seeded with fixed ids so two devices seeding before they sync upsert the same rows instead of leaving duplicates.
Data sits in the shared database under finances, finances:categories and finances:wallets — a prefix convention rather than distinct tables.
What exists today is a ledger. A ledger tells you what happened; a tracker tells you whether it's going the way you meant. Most of the roadmap is the distance between the two.

saveCategory and removeCategory exist in store.ts and are called from nowhere, so the user is locked to the seeded categories forever. Wallets got this screen and categories didn't — 'a bug wearing a feature's clothes', and mostly a copy of Wallets.tsx.

There is currently no way to find a past transaction except paging Month backwards. A search over note and category name plus a from/to filter fits the existing pure-function pattern in money.ts and needs no data model change.
The sheet closing and the row appearing is the entire feedback today; a brief highlight on the new row would close the loop.

The biggest single addition and the one that fits the app's name: a cap you check yourself against, one month at a time. Month already computes categoryBreakdown — a budget is that number against a target.
A ledger that inserts rows you didn't authorise is a ledger you stop trusting, and trusting it is the whole point. Due items appear as a 'confirm these' strip on Log.
Answers 'is this getting worse', which no current screen can.
Partly a backup, partly trust — an app holding your money history should have a visible exit door. Cheap: a pure function over Txn[] plus a download.
The tricky part is that a repayment is both a debt event and a wallet movement; double-counting it would break the totals the same way transfers would have.
A target amount and date against a wallet; small if it leans on walletBalances. Open design question: is a goal a property of a wallet or its own thing?
The Instant app already has $files, so the storage exists; the cost is UI and sync weight, not backend.

Breaks the architecture rather than adding to it: owner-scoped permissions allow a row only when auth.id == data.owner, and split expenses need rows visible to two accounts. That's a permissions redesign, not a feature.
money.ts hardcodes en-PH and PHP. A second currency means a currency per wallet, a rate at time of transaction, and a decision about what a cross-currency 'total' even means. Large.

Deliberately generic so new collections need no schema push — finances:budgets, finances:recurring, finances:debts all just work under the existing prefix convention. Called out as a real advantage worth spending.
A row is allowed only when auth.id == data.owner. Every roadmap item fits under that rule except shared expenses.
Budgets and recurring items both point at a category id. walletBalances already handles the equivalent for deleted wallets by skipping unknown ids — the same discipline applies.
Minimal shell: a #root div and a module script. Description is 'Daily bread, accounted for.'

Android reads display/standalone from the manifest, but iOS historically needed apple-mobile-web-app-* and still uses them for the home-screen label and status bar. Without apple-mobile-web-app-capable an older iPhone opens the app with browser chrome, which defeats the point of installing it.
Two theme-color meta tags keyed to prefers-color-scheme: #F4EFE6 light, #1E1A17 dark — the Tiswell palette carried into the browser chrome.
Loaded from a remote stylesheet with preconnect hints — a network dependency in an app whose stated constraint is offline-first.
The shell boots the app from /dev/main.tsx rather than src/, indicating a dev-harness entry rather than the production app root.
A deliberately separate Worker so the PWA's own deploy (../wrangler.jsonc) stays pure static assets. It is the only place the Anthropic API key lives, and the key never reaches the browser.

'200 on Jollibee today' returns a transaction draft that the add sheet opens on the review panel. Nothing is written until the user confirms — the same approve-don't-auto-write stance applied to parsing.
Response shape is { draft, confidence } where draft carries kind, amountCents, categoryId and note, and is passed straight to <AddSheet draft={draft} />.

The prompt, the id-pinned schema and the validation all live in ../src/parse.ts, shared verbatim between Worker and app and unit-tested in ../src/parse.test.ts — so the client and server can never disagree about the draft shape.

Body carries sentence plus the live category and wallet lists from useCategories()/useWallets(), and an optional today for resolving 'today'/'yesterday' in the user's local date. Sending the live lists is what lets the model pin real ids instead of inventing names.

It ships in the PWA bundle so it is a soft gate, not a hard secret: with the CORS origin allowlist it deters casual abuse of a paid endpoint. Cloudflare Access in front of the Worker is the noted path to a hard gate.
Stored as a Wrangler secret in Cloudflare, never in the repo. This is the one credential that must stay server-side, and separating the Worker from the static PWA deploy is what guarantees it.
Configured in worker/wrangler.jsonc and must be edited to the real PWA origins before deploying; pairs with APP_TOKEN as the second half of the soft gate.

The Add sheet flattens every parent/subcategory pair, sorts by the `uses` counter, and shows only the top six plus an 'All categories...' escape hatch. The six most-logged things are reachable in one tap, so the common case never opens the full picker; the list re-ranks itself as habits change instead of needing manual pinning.

Level two of the category sheet leads with a 'Log to <Parent> only - sort it out later' row, and logIt tags the meta as 'no subcategory'. A hurried log that gets sorted later beats a log that never happened, so subcategory is never allowed to block the save.

Adding a parent past twelve is refused outright with 'Twelve parents is the ceiling. Add a subcategory instead.' Parents are picked on every log, so they must fit one screen without scrolling; the running count hint under the list keeps the 8-12 band visible while editing.

Recording a payment on an Owed card calls addTx with the meta 'Transfer - not a category' and no category colour. Cash drops and the obligation drops by the same amount, so nothing was consumed; giving it a category would make the reports lie.

A single NOTIFS array drives both the Home strips (entries flagged strip:1) and the bell panel, with renderAll fanning out to both plus the badge count. Dismissal sets one flag, so the two surfaces can never disagree and dismissed items stay restorable.

The Add sheet ships its own 3x4 pad with a decimal guard (max two decimal places, nine digits) and a hardware-keyboard fallback listener. The system keyboard covers the category grid and forces typing blind; a custom pad keeps amount, note, wallet, and categories all visible at once.

The single `floor:true` entry in ALLOT renders as a highlighted card reading 'Floor met - at least 10% of income set apart', while all others read 'Ceiling - at most this much'. This one inversion is what carries the stewardship function without needing a separate God/Needs/Wants classification.

Wallets sums six balances into one 'Everything' figure; the Owed summary sits below it in its own panel with the note that it is not part of the total. Rolling loans in would turn the number into net worth, which answers a different question from 'what can I spend today'.

A single :root block defines night/dusk/raised/bone/muted/hair plus accent, pos, and over as semantic roles rather than literal colour names, so every surface in the prototype reads from one declaration.

Manna's .env must carry the same InstantDB app id as Tiswell's - that identical string is the entire mechanism by which two apps on two origins become one database. Sign-in is a magic code; afterwards the session persists and reads are served locally, so the app still opens and captures with no signal.

Two theme-color tags keyed on prefers-color-scheme (#F4EFE6 light, #1E1A17 dark) so the browser chrome flips with the system before React boots - nothing is stored and there is no flash of the wrong theme.
pnpm blocks post-install build scripts by default; only esbuild (Vite's bundler) and sharp (the icon generator behind `pnpm icons`) are allowed to run theirs.

No mini-app is compiled in. Every app is its own project on its own server, added as a Home tile by pasting a link (localhost dev servers included). Sharing the database used to be the reason to compile an app in; a shared Instant app plus the postMessage session handshake removed that reason.
A calm shell hosting one mini-app per life area, added over time, rather than one monolithic life app - so each area can ship independently while the shell stays constant.
Ship the smallest useful thing, then grow. Highest-priority guiding principle - it is what keeps the empty registry and the no-'coming soon'-tiles rule acceptable.
Every mini-app consumes the shared tokens and components so the whole hosted collection feels like one app rather than a launcher for strangers.

Adding a mini-app must never require editing shell internals - only registering a manifest. This is what makes the shell stable as apps accumulate, and it is why the shell renders tiles and routes from the registry and nothing else.
Soft, rounded, earthy, quiet - the app should feel like an exhale. Drives the no-sharp-corners rule, low warm shadows, 150-250ms motion, and reduced-motion support.

React 18 + TS on Vite, Tailwind v4 CSS-first tokens, vite-plugin-pwa, InstantDB, React Router with lazy per-mini-app routes, Cloudflare Pages, pnpm. Dexie/IndexedDB was the Phase 0-1 storage and survives only to migrate old devices.

A single Vite app organized like a platform via @ui / @data / @miniapps / @shell aliases instead of a pnpm workspace monorepo, deliberately avoiding workspace overhead until it is actually needed. Manna aliases @ui and @data straight at these source folders, which is why src/data must never import from @shell.
id, name, icon, accent, route, storageNamespace, component. Accent is a token name only, never a hex, so a mini-app cannot break the shared palette or the dark theme.
Home maps the registry to a Tile grid and App.tsx maps it to lazy Routes. Only live mini-apps appear - no 'coming soon' tiles, ever.

Every read and write in the app goes through list/get/put/remove/subscribe/snapshot/ready; no feature may import the backend directly. That single choke point is why swapping Dexie for InstantDB changed nothing above the data layer - the interface only grew subscribe/snapshot/ready, because a sync engine can say *when* data changed and a promise-only shape could not.
Callers subscribe through hooks instead of re-fetching after a write, because the sync engine already knows when data changed - including changes written by another origin or another device.
Every read is served from an in-memory copy because db.queryOnce throws when offline. Being backend-free is also what makes it the part that can be unit tested.
One auth subscription and one query subscription feeding the mirror, exporting the singleton `data: TiswellData`.
Tiswell holds the session and hands it to embedded apps over postMessage, origin-checked in both directions - one sign-in covers both origins.
Drains each origin's old Dexie database exactly once. local.ts and the dexie dependency exist only for this and should be deleted once every device has run it.
One `records` namespace keyed "${ns}:${id}" because Instant keys entities by a single UUID and two namespaces may legitimately hold the same record id.
Everything denied unless auth.id == data.owner. The app id ships in both client bundles by design, so these rules - not secrecy - are the guard.

Planned as Supabase plus a hand-rolled Dexie-Postgres mirror with updatedAt last-write-wins; shipped as InstantDB instead, so tombstones, LWW merge, pull cursors, and retry queues were never written at all. Tiswell and Manna sit on different origins where browser storage can never be shared, so a common backend was the only fix - and it bought one sign-in and cross-device sync on top of the original goal.

Single source of truth; components consume tokens only, never raw hex. Clay/umber/sage/sand neutrals, Quicksand display + Nunito Sans body, fully rounded controls. A literal hex, or a colour chosen only against light, is the way this system breaks.

Token names are roles, not literal colours - clay-50 means app background, umber-900 means ink. One prefers-color-scheme block redeclares the custom properties and both apps flip with no `dark:` variant anywhere in the codebase. It follows the system, so nothing is stored and there is no flash of the wrong theme before React boots. Dark is warm brown-black, not neutral charcoal, so clay and umber still read as themselves.

Three tokens exist only because a role that is single-valued in light splits in two in dark. `raised` must go lighter while the background goes darkest, or the selected segment recedes. `scrim` is the one place ink is a surface; inverting it would flash the screen white at night. `balance` is Manna's balance card, which left to invert would become a glaring cream slab and instead becomes raised warm green. Do not collapse them back.

A floating button visible in the shell and inside every mini-app opens a bottom sheet with one autofocused multiline input, saving straight to the `inbox` namespace. Capture must never require deciding where the thought belongs first.
Reached from a header badge showing the unfiled count; newest-first with relative dates. 'File into app' stays disabled until mini-apps exist.
With an empty registry it shows the Exhale mark, the words 'It is well.', and one line of copy - deliberately with no call to action.

Clay-200 rounded square with three softening strokes in umber, umber-light, and sage at descending weight and opacity - the visual statement of 'calm over clever'. The SVG is the source all PNG icon sizes are regenerated from.

The brand mark is the single source-of-truth vector for all Manna app icons: a 280x280 viewBox containing three stroked, open arcs drawn concentrically and uniformly scaled (1.6512) about the canvas centre. Nothing is filled; the logo is pure stroke with round line caps, so it stays legible at 32px and reads as a hand-drawn gesture rather than a corporate glyph. Because every raster icon is a render of this one file, colour or geometry changes propagate by re-exporting rather than by editing four assets.

Three concentric arcs of decreasing radius (75.75, 34.74, 18.95) each deliberately left open with a gap, reading inward from a near-complete outer ring to a small dark smile/bowl at the centre. The gaps mean no ring ever closes, giving a containment-and-provision reading (an open vessel, a portion set aside) that suits a stewardship log rather than a sealed 'balance' or 'total' symbol. The inward-shrinking repetition also mirrors the app's own two-level containment structure: an outer whole holding a smaller inner part.

Three muted earth strokes ordered by depth: sage/olive #9F9A77 on the outer ring, clay/tan #A2886E in the middle, dark walnut #5E4634 at the core, over a warm beige field. Value darkens as radius shrinks, so the eye is pulled to the centre without any accent or saturated colour. The palette is intentionally non-fintech: no green-for-gain, no red-for-loss, no blue trust-badge, which keeps the app from reading as a budgeting or banking tool and matches its framing as a personal log rather than a ledger of performance.

Every path uses fill="none" with a near-uniform stroke-width (7.9 / 7.4 / 7.9) and stroke-linecap="round". Holding the stroke weight almost constant across three very different radii is what makes the arcs read as one family instead of three unrelated rings, and the round caps prevent the open gaps from looking like clipped or broken geometry. This same stroke-weight discipline is what lets the mark sit beside the app's line-style Remix Icon category glyphs without looking heavier than them.

Raster render of the Manna mark at 192x192 on an opaque warm-beige field with slightly rounded corners, the standard small-size PWA manifest icon used for home-screen shortcuts and install prompts. The background is baked in rather than transparent so the mark never inherits an unpredictable launcher wallpaper behind its open arcs.

Large 512x512 render of the same mark, used for splash screens, install dialogs, and store-style listings. The artwork fills roughly 70 percent of the canvas edge to edge, which is correct for an 'any' purpose icon but too tight to survive a circular launcher crop, which is precisely why a separate maskable variant exists alongside it.

The same 512x512 mark rendered noticeably smaller within the canvas, with the beige field bleeding to all four edges. This is the purpose="maskable" manifest entry: Android and other launchers crop app icons to an arbitrary platform shape (circle, squircle, teardrop), and only a variant with deliberate margin survives that crop intact.

The mark is inset so it stays inside the central 80 percent safe circle of the icon canvas, leaving the outer band as sacrificial bleed. Compared against icon-512, the artwork is scaled down roughly 15-20 percent while the background extends fully to the edges. Without this inset the outermost sage ring, which is the mark's silhouette, would be shaved by any circular launcher mask and the logo would lose its defining outline.

The 192 + 512 + maskable-512 trio is the conventional minimum an installable PWA manifest must declare to satisfy install criteria across browsers and launchers. Manna is deliberately a PWA rather than a native app, so these four files are the entire app-identity surface: there is no store listing or native bundle to carry branding, and the home-screen icon is the only place the product is seen before it is opened.

Square master brand asset for Tiswell, the sibling application to Manna. Vertical lockup: the concentric-arc mark sits above a lowercase wordmark on a flat cream field, with no tagline, no border, and no drop shadow. The square 1:1 framing and generous margin make the same file usable as an avatar, store listing tile, or splash image without recomposition.

Set entirely in lowercase as 'tiswell' in a soft geometric sans with rounded terminals and wide letter tracking, coloured in the darkest brown of the palette. Lowercase-only and rounded terminals keep the tone domestic and unassuming rather than corporate, matching an app about possessions you already own.

The canonical vector source of the brand mark: four open, round-capped strokes of decreasing radius (72, 52, 33, 18) nested around a shared centre, each broken at a different angle so no ring closes. Built as pure stroked arcs with no fills and no text, so it scales to a 16px favicon and up to a 512px splash from one file. The innermost 18-radius arc is a half-circle read as a smile, turning the abstract nest of rings into a face at small sizes.

A four-step ramp — sage olive #9F9A77 outermost, tan #B6A284, warm brown #A2886E, dark brown #5E4634 innermost — over a cream field. The ramp darkens monotonically inward, so the innermost arc carries the most contrast and the eye lands on it first; that is what makes the smile legible at 192px where the outer rings blur into texture. Muted, low-saturation earth tones instead of a saturated brand hue keep the mark from competing with content.

The innermost path is the only arc drawn as an explicit open half-circle with sweep-flag 1 rather than a broken ring, and it is the heaviest stroke at 7.5 on the smallest radius. This is the payoff of the whole composition: at icon sizes the three outer rings read as an abstract nest, and the single dark curve at the centre resolves them into a face. It is also the one element the design cannot afford to lose to a maskable crop.

The whole group is wrapped in translate(140 140) scale(1.7373) translate(-140 -140), a scale about the artwork centre rather than the origin. The arcs were authored on a 280 canvas at their natural radii and then blown up 1.74x in place, deliberately pushing the outer sage ring past the viewBox edge so it bleeds off. Keeping the magnification as a transform instead of rewriting every path radius means the arc geometry stays editable in the units it was designed in.

The small-size member of the PWA manifest icon set: the concentric arc mark on an opaque cream square, sized for home-screen shortcuts and browser tab or task-switcher chrome. At this resolution the three outer rings compress toward each other and the dark smile is the only element still individually legible, which is exactly what the darkening colour ramp was built to guarantee.

The large-size manifest icon used for install prompts and splash screens. The mark is scaled nearly edge to edge with only a thin cream margin, because the 'any' purpose contract means the platform renders the square as authored and does not crop it.

Every raster export bakes in a solid cream background even though the vector source has none. A transparent PNG would let the mark's pale sage and tan arcs disappear against a light launcher wallpaper or a light browser theme, and the palette has no dark anchor besides the small smile. Shipping the field as part of the bitmap makes contrast independent of wherever the platform places the icon.

A mid-size raster of the mark alone, without the wordmark, on the cream field. Sits outside the numbered manifest icon sizes, so it is the in-app or header usage rather than a platform install asset. The mark is inset further from the edges than in icon-512, giving it the breathing room a UI element needs when a launcher tile does not.

The 'maskable' purpose variant for Android adaptive icons, where the launcher may clip the square to a circle, squircle, rounded square, or teardrop at its own discretion. Identical artwork to icon-512 but noticeably reduced in scale with a wider cream border, so the crop eats only background.

The mark is shrunk to sit inside roughly the central 80 percent circle rather than filling the square, which is why the maskable export cannot simply be the 'any' icon reused. A shared file would either waste space on launchers that do not crop or lose the outer sage ring on launchers that crop to a circle; two exports from one vector source resolves the conflict at build time instead of at runtime. The extra cream margin is doing real work here, not padding.
